setupSteps: Lay the mat lengthwise on the floor, with enough space for one leg to point at the ceiling. Avoid a bed or sofa: the soft surface lets the pelvis sink.
Get a strap, belt, long towel or dupatta about 1.5–2 m long (est.). Fold a towel lengthwise so it does not twist.
Sit on the mat, then lie on your back. Head on the mat or on a thin folded towel if your chin pokes up.

Bottom leg (beginner default): bend the non-stretching knee and put that foot flat on the mat, hip-width from the other leg. This keeps the low back relaxed (South Tees NHS; Healthwise). Harder option: bottom leg straight on the floor, toes to the ceiling.
Bend the stretching knee toward your chest and loop the strap around the ball or arch of that foot (Liforme), not the toes.
Hold one end of the strap in each hand, elbows relaxed on the floor or bent, shoulders down.
Lie on your back in a doorway, with the stretching leg on the door-frame side.

Shuffle your bottom close to the wall beside the frame and rest the heel of the stretching leg up the wall; the other leg goes straight through the doorway along the floor (Healthwise doorway stretch; Mayo Clinic wall stretch).
Move your hips closer to the wall for more stretch, further away for less.
Stand facing a low step, bottom stair or sturdy footstool (about ankle to mid-shin height, est.). Higher is not better: a high step tips the pelvis back.
Hold a wall, rail or table edge for balance if needed.
Place the heel of the stretching leg on the step, knee straight but soft, toes up and relaxed. The standing leg is straight under the hip with a soft knee, foot pointing forward.
Hands on the hips or on the thigh of the raised leg (never pressing down on the knee).
Use a sturdy chair without wheels (Mayo Clinic Care Network); push it against a wall or desk if it slides on tiles.
Sit near the front edge of the seat, feet flat.
Slide the stretching leg forward so the knee is straight and the heel rests on the floor, toes up. The other foot stays flat with the knee bent at about 90°.
Sit tall: weight on both sitting bones, hands on the bent-knee thigh or the front of the seat.

steps.title: Lie down and loop the strap
steps.action: lie on your back, bottom-leg knee bent, foot flat; loop the strap around the ball of the other foot with that knee bent toward the chest.
steps.feel: back of the pelvis and shoulders resting evenly on the mat.
steps.visualCheck: side view, head, shoulders and pelvis on the mat; front view, strap ends held evenly in both hands.

steps.title: Straighten the leg toward the ceiling
steps.action: breathe out and slowly press the foot up into the strap, straightening the knee as much as is comfortable.
steps.feel: a gradual pull starting in the middle of the back of the thigh.
steps.breathing: breathe out as the leg rises.
steps.visualCheck: side view, leg rising roughly toward vertical; a soft knee bend is fine.

steps.title: Find the first point of stretch
steps.action: stop raising the leg as soon as you feel mild tension (the ACSM "point of tightness or slight discomfort"). Many beginners stop well before vertical (45–70° from the floor, est.), and that is fine.
steps.feel: steady tension in the belly of the hamstring, not at the back of the knee or in the buttock crease.
steps.visualCheck: pelvis still flat on the mat; the bottom of the pelvis has not curled up off the floor.

steps.title: Set the pelvis and back
steps.action: let both buttocks stay heavy on the mat and keep the natural small gap under the low back. If the tailbone curls up, lower the leg a little (Yoga Journal: lower the leg or bend the knee if needed).
steps.feel: low back relaxed, not pressed flat or arched hard.
steps.visualCheck: side view, hip bones level; the bottom leg's knee not drifting.

steps.title: Relax the shoulders, arms and ankle
steps.action: keep the elbows soft and shoulders on the floor; let the strap hold the leg so the arms do little work (Liforme). Keep the ankle relaxed in a neutral position, not pulled hard toward you.
steps.feel: neck and shoulders soft; stretch stays in the back of the thigh.
steps.visualCheck: front view, shoulders level, chin not lifted toward the ceiling.

steps.title: Hold
steps.action: stay still. Do not bounce or pull in jerks.
steps.feel: mild, steady stretch (stretch sensation about 3–5 out of 10, est.) that eases slightly as you hold. Overall effort is light: 3–4 on the ACSM 0–10 perceived-exertion scale (= Borg 9–11 on the 6–20 scale).
steps.breathing: slow breathing, about 5–6 breaths in 30 seconds (est.); never hold the breath.
steps.visualCheck: no shaking in the leg, pelvis and head still on the mat.

steps.title: Optional: ease a little deeper
steps.action: if the stretch has faded, breathe out and draw the leg a few centimetres closer, or straighten the knee a little more.
steps.feel: the tension returns to the same mild level, never sharp.
steps.visualCheck: pelvis still flat; if the tailbone lifts, go back.

steps.title: Release
steps.action: bend the knee, bring it toward the chest, slip off the strap and lower the foot to the mat.
steps.feel: the stretch fades; no lingering pain.
steps.visualCheck: foot lowered with control, not dropped.

steps.title: Switch sides
steps.action: loop the strap on the other foot and repeat steps 2–8. Do 2 rounds per leg (section 7).
steps.feel: the two sides may differ; that is common.

steps.title: Get up safely
steps.action: roll onto your side, push up with your hands to sitting, then stand.
steps.feel: no strain in the back; no dizziness.
steps.visualCheck: no sit-up "jack-knife" straight from the back.

commonMistakes.title: Rounding the back to reach the toes
commonMistakes.text: Rounding the back to reach the toes. It moves the stretch from the hamstrings to the spine and loads the low back; López-Miñarro's work shows a good hamstring stretch shows up as pelvic tilt, not more spinal rounding. Fix: hinge from the hips with a flat back; reach less far; use the supine version.

commonMistakes.title: Bouncing
commonMistakes.text: Bouncing. Jerky movement can over-stretch tissue and triggers muscle guarding. Fix: move slowly into a still hold (ACSM static stretching).

commonMistakes.title: Stretching into pain
commonMistakes.text: Stretching into pain. Sharp pain, pain behind the knee or tingling down the leg is not a useful stretch. Fix: back off to mild tension; stop if pain persists (Healthwise; South Tees NHS: aim for a gentle pull, no need to force the range).

commonMistakes.title: Pulling the toes hard toward the shin and dropping the chin
commonMistakes.text: Pulling the toes hard toward the shin and dropping the chin. Adds tension on the sciatic nerve rather than the muscle; if tingling or burning appears, this is the likely cause (Prehab Guys). Fix: relax the ankle and keep the head neutral.

commonMistakes.title: Locking the knee or pushing it down with a hand
commonMistakes.text: Locking the knee or pushing it down with a hand. Stresses the back of the knee joint. Fix: soft knee; hands on the thigh, never the kneecap.

commonMistakes.title: Lifting the pelvis or head in the supine version
commonMistakes.text: Lifting the pelvis or head in the supine version. The tailbone curls up and the stretch disappears into the back. Fix: lower the leg until the pelvis rests down; head on the mat.

commonMistakes.title: Too high a step in the standing version
commonMistakes.text: Too high a step in the standing version. A table-height leg rest tips the pelvis back and rounds the back. Fix: use a step at ankle to mid-shin height.

commonMistakes.title: Long static holds right before sprinting or heavy lifting
commonMistakes.text: Long static holds right before sprinting or heavy lifting. Holds of 60 s or more per muscle can briefly reduce strength and power (Behm et al. 2016 review); holds under 60 s inside a full warm-up have trivial effects. Fix: before workouts use short holds or leg swings; save longer holds for after.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Raises tension and blood pressure. Fix: slow nasal breathing throughout.

safetyNotes: Low back pain: use the supine version (back supported) with the bottom knee bent. South Tees NHS advises people with a back problem to check with their physiotherapist first. Avoid standing toe-touches with a rounded back. Stop if back pain increases.

Sciatica or leg pain that runs below the knee, numbness or tingling: this may be nerve sensitivity, not tight muscle. If changing the ankle or neck position changes the symptoms, the nerve is likely involved (Prehab Guys; clinical rule of thumb, not a validated test). Keep the ankle relaxed and the head down; stop if tingling appears; get assessed.
Recent hamstring strain or tear: no stretching in the first 2–4 days; start gentle stretches only when normal walking is pain-free; stretches should never hurt (Northern Care Alliance NHS; nidirect).
Knee problems: keep a soft knee; never press on the kneecap; pain behind the knee means ease off.

Hip replacement (especially posterior approach): the upper body and thigh must not come closer than 90°, usually for about 6 weeks or until the surgeon says otherwise (Kaiser Permanente; Northwestern Medicine). Supine leg raises past 90° hip flexion and forward bends break this rule; ask your surgeon.

Osteoporosis: avoid forward bending with a rounded spine, toe touches and twisting forward bends (New York State and New Jersey osteoporosis guidance). Use the supine strap version with a neutral spine.
High blood pressure: stretching is suitable; keep breathing and get up slowly from the floor. Avoid breath-holding.

Pregnancy: avoid lying flat on the back after the first trimester (about 12 weeks; ACOG guidance as reported by secondary sources), so use the seated or standing versions; joints are looser (relaxin), so do not push beyond your pre-pregnancy range.
Recent surgery: wait for clearance (abdominal, hip, knee, spine or eye surgery).

Stop immediately if you feel: sharp or tearing pain in the thigh or behind the knee; tingling, burning or numbness down the leg; back pain that increases; dizziness when getting up; a pop or sudden weakness.
Gym etiquette: use the stretching area or a mat out of walkways; do not hog a bench or squat rack for a heel-on-step stretch; wipe mats and straps after use.

Hold time: 10–30 s (ACSM), ~30 s (Mayo), 15–30 s up to 1 min (Healthwise towel), 30–60 s (US lying-towel guides), 1–6 min (Healthwise doorway). Bandy found 30 s = 60 s. We chose 30 s × 2 per leg for beginners; longer doorway holds only for intermediate/advanced flexibility goals.

Which version first: standing toe-touch versions are common in Indian school PE, but they invite back rounding and are flagged for osteoporosis and back pain. We teach the supine strap version first (back supported, Mayo/Healthwise/NHS), with standing and seated versions as alternatives.
Bottom leg bent or straight (supine): NHS and Healthwise start with the bottom knee bent; yoga sources keep it straight and pressing down. Beginners bend; straight is a progression.

Ankle pulled up or relaxed: pulling the toes toward the shin increases the calf and nerve stretch; nerve-tension sources advise against it for sensitive people. We default to a relaxed, neutral ankle.

Stretching before exercise: long holds (≥ 60 s) can briefly reduce strength and power; short holds within a full warm-up have trivial effects. We keep pre-workout holds ≤ 30 s and put longer holds after training.
Hamstring stretching for back pain: a 2024 review supports range-of-motion gains in radiating back pain; effect on pain is less certain. Framed as "may help", with physio check first.
